title: Run Your Project the Way a Grid Operator Runs the System
summary: Risk management is not a list of worries; it is a working system that names each risk, gives it an owner and a trigger, and plans the response before it is needed. The grid operator's N-1 rule, that the system must survive the loss of any single element, is the right test for a development project too.
body:
Risk management is not a list of worries. It is a working system: every significant risk named, sized, owned, watched for a trigger and given a planned response, so that the loss of any single element does not bring the project down.

Recall

Q. What does a performance bond cover after a contractor default?

A. The excess of the cost to complete over the unpaid contract balance, up to the penal sum, subject to the bond's wording and conditions.

Q. In Week 78, what are the three questions of the allocation test?

A. Who can control the risk, who can price it and who can carry it. The best owner of a risk passes all three.

Q. In Week 72, what is beneficial ownership?

A. The real people who ultimately own or control an entity, behind any chain of companies, trusts or nominees. Banks and regulators increasingly require it to be identified and verified.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you have spent years in operations where the question was never whether something would fail, but what the system would do when it did. A reliability coordinator does not hope the largest generator stays online; the system is run so that if it trips, the lights stay on. Development projects are usually run the opposite way: the plan assumes everything goes right, and the risks are listed in an appendix nobody reads. This week turns your operating instinct into a project discipline.

The N-1 test

In plain English: ask which single failure would stop the project, and make sure the answer is none.

The professional framing comes straight from power-system operations. The N-1 criterion requires that the system can lose any one element, a line, a transformer, a generating unit, and still operate within limits, with a plan ready to restore margin before the next failure. Translate it to a project. The elements are the contractor, the lender, the anchor buyer or tenant, the critical supplier, the key consultant, the approval that is still pending, and you. For each, ask: if it failed tomorrow, does the project survive, and is the plan written down?

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A 20,000,000 dollar project has one general contractor with thin working capital, a construction loan of 13,000,000 dollars with no alternative lender in view, and a single supplier of a custom facade with a 26-week lead time. Run N-1. Lose the contractor: a performance bond of 50 percent and a pre-qualified second contractor make the project survivable, though late. Lose the facade supplier: no second source has been approved and the lead time is half a year, so the project stops for six months. That is an N-1 violation. The fix is not to worry about it. It is to approve a second facade supplier during design, or to buy the long-lead items early with title passing to you, while there is still time.

The risk register: a tool, not a document

A risk register is a table with one row per significant risk. The columns that make it work are these: a description of the cause and effect; probability and impact, before and after the planned response; a named owner, one person, not a firm; the response; the trigger that tells you the risk is becoming real; and the date it was last reviewed.

Probability and impact are often scored on a simple scale, say 1 to 5 each, and multiplied to rank risks. That ranking is useful for attention. It is not a number to put in a budget. For money, you need impact in dollars and days, and probability as a percentage, which is where the Monte Carlo work later this week begins.

Responses come in four kinds. Avoid: change the plan so the risk cannot happen. Reduce: lower its probability or impact. Transfer: move it to a party that can carry it, by contract, insurance or bond, the subject of the last two weeks. Accept: keep it, knowingly, and fund it in contingency.

Say that out loud now.

One name per risk, one trigger per risk, and the response written before the trigger fires.

Triggers: the part most registers leave out

In operations you do not wait for a line to trip; you watch loading against a limit and act at an alarm point. A project risk needs the same: a leading indicator and a threshold at which the planned response starts.

A second worked example, hypothetical, on contractor default. The leading indicators are known: subcontractors complaining of late payment, the contractor asking to reduce retainage, billing running ahead of your own estimate of work in place, key site staff leaving, and the contractor's bonding capacity or credit rating falling. Write the triggers. Amber: two subcontractor complaints in a month, or billing more than 5 percentage points ahead of verified progress. Response at amber: weekly payment checks with subcontractors, joint cheques or direct payment where the contract allows, a meeting with the contractor's director and a call to the surety's representative to understand the contractor's standing. Red: a missed payroll, liens registered, or a request for an unsecured advance. Response at red: written notice under the contract, the default procedure from Week 79 and the second contractor called. These thresholds are practice, not standards; set your own.

Notice that the triggers turn a vague worry into a decision the owner made in advance, in a calm month, which is the only kind of month when good decisions about default get made.

How the best do it

Owners with mature risk practice hold a short risk review on a fixed rhythm, often monthly, separate from the progress meeting. The top ten risks are reviewed by their owners, triggers are checked against the latest data, closed risks are removed and new ones added, and contingency is re-forecast against what remains. They also run a pre-mortem at each stage gate. A small developer can copy the rhythm with a one-hour monthly meeting and a register of no more than twenty rows. A short register that is used beats a long one that is not.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: how contingency spent, insurance recovered and costs written off are treated depends on local rules; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: the register shows what the owner knew and when, so keep it honest and dated. Banking: lenders and their monitors increasingly ask to see the register; a good one builds credibility. Governance: each risk has one named owner, and the board or investment committee sees the top risks every quarter. Estate: you are an element in the N-1 test; key-person risk needs a written succession plan for the project. Exit: a buyer's diligence will ask for open risks and their status at sale.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor or cost consultant, on the dollar impacts; scheduler, on the time impacts.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a register that is written once for the lender and never used: risks with no owners, no triggers and no review date, so the project meets each risk as a surprise. The control is the monthly review, one named owner per risk, and a trigger for every risk in the top ten.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner lists fifty risks, scores them all as medium and calls it management. Rank ruthlessly, work the top ten, and ask the N-1 question of every critical element.

Callback

In Week 2, Ford and Kema taught OODA and the after-action review: observe, orient, decide, act, then learn. A risk register with triggers is that loop built into the project in advance. The trigger is the observation, the planned response is the decision already made, and the monthly review is the after-action learning.

Recap

Run the project like the grid: it must survive the loss of any single element. Name each significant risk, size it in dollars and days, give it one owner, a response and a trigger, and review it monthly. Avoid, reduce, transfer or accept, and fund what you accept.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: Carillion in 2018, and what owners learn when their contractor fails.
checklist: I can name every single element whose failure would stop the project.
For each critical element I have a written plan to continue without it.
Every top-ten risk has one named owner, not a firm.
Every top-ten risk has a leading indicator and a trigger threshold.
Every risk has a response: avoid, reduce, transfer or accept.
Accepted risks are funded in contingency, in dollars and days.
I hold a risk review monthly, separate from the progress meeting.
Key-person risk, including my own, has a written succession plan.
head: Field checklist
speak: Risk management is a working system, not a list of worries. I borrow the grid operator's N-1 rule: the project must survive the loss of any single element, whether the contractor, the lender, a critical supplier, a key consultant, a pending approval or me. If losing a facade supplier with a 26-week lead time would stop the job for six months, that is an N-1 violation, and I fix it in design with a second approved source or early purchase. My risk register has one row per risk: cause and effect, probability and impact in dollars and days, one named owner, a response, a trigger and a review date. Responses are avoid, reduce, transfer or accept, and what I accept I fund in contingency. The triggers matter most. For contractor default I watch late subcontractor payments, early retainage requests and billing ahead of work, and I decide the amber and red responses in a calm month, not in a crisis.
terms: Risk register — a table of significant risks with cause, probability, impact, owner, response, trigger and review date.
Trigger — a leading indicator and threshold at which a planned risk response begins.
N-1 criterion — the operating rule that a system must continue within limits after losing any single element.

hostile.q: Your register lists forty risks. Which one would stop this project, and what happens if it does?
hostile.a: The single point of failure today is the facade supplier: one source and a 26-week lead time. We have approved a second supplier this month and are placing the first order early, with title passing to us, so a failure costs weeks, not half a year. The next is the contractor, where we hold a performance and payment bond and a pre-qualified second contractor. The other thirty-eight are real but survivable, and each has an owner and a trigger.

title: Carillion, 2018: When the Contractor Is the Single Point of Failure
summary: Carillion, a large British construction and services contractor, issued a major profit warning in July 2017 and went into compulsory liquidation in January 2018, leaving projects including two large hospitals unfinished and a long supply chain unpaid. Seven forensic steps, taken from the owner's side, show how a counterparty failure becomes a project failure.
body:
When Carillion collapsed in January 2018, its clients learned that a contractor's balance sheet is part of the project's structure. The owners who suffered least were the ones who had treated contractor failure as a risk to manage, not an event that could not happen.

Recall

Q. What is the N-1 criterion, applied to a project?

A. The project must survive the loss of any single element, such as the contractor, the lender or a critical supplier, with a written plan ready to continue without it.

Q. In Week 78, why is a risk transfer only worth what the receiving party can pay?

A. Because a clause moving a risk to a contractor protects you only as far as its money, insurance and security reach. A judgment against an insolvent company is a piece of paper.

Q. In Week 72, what is source of funds checking?

A. Establishing where the specific money in a transaction came from, to be satisfied it is legitimate, as distinct from source of wealth, which asks how a person came to have their wealth overall.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me because this is a case about counterparty risk, which is how a lender thinks about every relationship on a project. I will keep to facts that are well established in the public record and avoid figures I cannot verify. Where I draw a lesson about owners in general, I say so; individual clients' circumstances differed, and some of the detail of who held what protection is not something I can confirm.

1. Timeline

Carillion was one of the largest construction and facilities services contractors in the United Kingdom, with a large book of public and private contracts. In July 2017 it issued a profit warning that included a major provision against the value of several construction contracts, and its share price fell sharply. Further warnings followed in the autumn. On 15 January 2018 the company entered compulsory liquidation. Projects were left incomplete, among them two large new hospitals, and subcontractors and suppliers across the country were left owed money. In May 2018 two committees of the House of Commons published a joint report sharply critical of the board, the company's accounting and its auditors, and of the oversight of a contractor so many public services depended on.

2. Key decisions

From the owner's side, three decisions recur across the public account. Awarding large, fixed-price contracts at margins that left little room for error. Continuing to place work with the same contractor after visible warnings. And, for some clients, relying on one contractor for many services at once, so that a single failure touched many projects together.

3. Assumptions

The central assumption was that a contractor of that size and history would not fail, or would be rescued if it did. Size felt like strength. The company's published accounts, later criticised, supported that belief, and a fixed price felt like a transfer of risk to a party that could carry it. Rule 78 from two weeks ago is the corrective: a transfer is worth what the receiving party can pay, and a thin margin on a large fixed price is a sign of a party that may not be able to.

4. Incentives

Clients were rewarded for the lowest price and for showing that risk had been passed to the private sector. A contractor under pressure to keep revenue growing had an incentive to bid low and to recover margin later through claims and changes. Long payment terms to suppliers helped the contractor's cash position at the supply chain's expense, which the parliamentary report criticised. Each party's incentive made the system more fragile and made the fragility harder to see.

Say that out loud now.

A contractor's balance sheet is part of my project's structure.

5. Warning signs ignored

The July 2017 profit warning was public and large. So were the later warnings and the fall in the share price. On the ground, the signs that precede most contractor failures, slower payment to subcontractors, staff departures and disputes over claims, are the ones owners should watch for on any project. The general lesson for owners, which the public record supports, is that warnings visible to markets months in advance did not translate into contingency plans fast enough in many places.

6. Point of no return

For a client, the point of no return was the date of liquidation itself, because after it no negotiated rescue of an individual contract was possible and every project moved straight to re-procurement. The months between the first warning and that date were the window in which an owner could act: tighten payment controls, verify subcontractor payment, secure documents and design information, confirm bond and insurance positions, line up a replacement and plan the handover.

7. Root cause

The root cause, at the level that matters for you, was a risk system that did not treat the contractor's survival as a risk at all. The failure of the counterparty carrying the largest share of the project's risk was not named, owned, watched or planned for. Once that element failed, the project had no N-1 margin.

Roman's view: what an owner could have done

Roman frames this as a lender would. A worked example, hypothetical, for a single owner with one 30,000,000 dollar contract with a large contractor. Before award: a financial review of the contractor beyond its size, including margin trend, cash conversion and the value of claims it carries in its accounts; a performance bond and payment bond from a separate surety; and a contract requiring the contractor to assign subcontracts and hand over design information on termination. During the job: a trigger on the contractor's public warnings, and on subcontractor payment. At the first warning: weekly payment verification, an updated plan for a replacement contractor, and an inventory of the drawings, warranties and materials the owner would need to restart. None of this stops a contractor failing. It changes how long the site stands idle and how much of the cost to complete the owner must find.

A second worked example, hypothetical. Suppose the owner is prepared and restarts with a replacement in 12 weeks; unprepared, it takes 30. At a daily cost of delay of 10,000 dollars, the difference of 18 weeks is 126 days, about 1,260,000 dollars, before any increase in the price to complete. Preparation is cheap by comparison.

The prevention rule

Rule 80: Treat the failure of your most important counterparty as a planned event: name it in the risk register, give it an owner, watch its leading indicators against written triggers, and keep a tested plan to continue the project without it.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, on termination, assignment and step-in provisions; accountant or credit analyst, on the contractor's financial review.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is confusing a counterparty's size with its strength. The control is a financial review at award, bonds from an independent surety, and triggers tied to public warnings and to subcontractor payment, reviewed monthly.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads a contractor's profit warning as the contractor's problem. It is yours. Treat it as an amber trigger the day it is published.

Callback

In Week 46, Ford and Roman's first post-mortem covered leverage spirals and guarantee calls: how a party with thin margins and heavy obligations can look healthy until cash runs out. Carillion is the same pattern on the contractor's side of the table, and the owner who learned the first lesson will recognise the second.

Recap

Carillion issued a large profit warning in July 2017 and entered compulsory liquidation on 15 January 2018, leaving projects unfinished and suppliers unpaid. The lesson for owners is that a contractor's survival is a risk to name, watch and plan for. Rule 80 makes counterparty failure a planned event.

Next: Sage on The Money: how a Monte Carlo view of risk sets contingency, and what that does to equity and returns.
checklist: I review a contractor's finances at award, not only its size and history.
I require performance and payment bonds from a surety independent of the contractor.
My contract requires assignment of subcontracts and handover of design information on termination.
I treat a contractor's public profit warning as an amber trigger the day it appears.
I verify subcontractor payment directly when any warning appears.
I keep an inventory of the drawings, warranties and materials needed to restart.
I have a replacement contractor plan reviewed at least quarterly.
head: Field checklist
speak: Carillion was one of Britain's largest construction and services contractors. It issued a major profit warning in July 2017, more warnings followed, and on 15 January 2018 it went into compulsory liquidation, leaving projects, including two large hospitals, unfinished and suppliers unpaid. In May 2018 a joint parliamentary report criticised its board, accounting and auditors. For an owner, the lesson is that a contractor's balance sheet is part of the project's structure. Clients assumed a contractor that size would not fail, and that a fixed price had transferred the risk. But a transfer is worth only what the receiving party can pay. The window to act was the months between warning and liquidation: verify subcontractor payment, secure design information, confirm bonds and line up a replacement. Rule 80: treat the failure of your most important counterparty as a planned event, named, owned, watched against triggers and backed by a tested plan.
terms: Counterparty risk — the risk that a party you depend on fails to perform or to pay.
Profit warning — a public statement by a listed company that results will be materially worse than expected.
Compulsory liquidation — a court-ordered winding up of an insolvent company, after which its contracts cannot be rescued by negotiation with it.

hostile.q: Your contractor has just issued a profit warning. Why should I keep funding draws?
hostile.a: Because the work is verified, and stopping draws now would push a weakened contractor towards failure. But I have moved to amber. From this week I verify subcontractor payment directly before each draw, the monitor checks billing against work in place on quantities, I have confirmed the bonds with the surety and asked for its view of the contractor, and the replacement plan is updated. If any red trigger fires, a missed payroll, liens or a request for an unsecured advance, I issue notice and you will hear from me the same day.

rule: Rule 80: Treat the failure of your most important counterparty as a planned event: name it in the risk register, give it an owner, watch its leading indicators against written triggers, and keep a tested plan to continue the project without it.

title: Contingency Is a Confidence Level You Choose
summary: A contingency figure is a choice about how confident you want to be that the budget will hold. Choosing it from a risk-based distribution, rather than a flat percentage, changes the budget, the loan, the equity and the return. And money that is not in the budget when a risk happens is paid by equity alone.
body:
A contingency is not a percentage you add because everyone does. It is a confidence level you choose: the chance that your budget will hold. Choose it from your own risks, and know that any overrun beyond it is paid by equity alone.

Recall

Q. What was Rule 80?

A. Treat the failure of your most important counterparty as a planned event: name it in the register, give it an owner, watch its leading indicators against written triggers, and keep a tested plan to continue without it.

Q. In Week 78, how do you compare a risk premium with the cost of keeping a risk?

A. Compare the premium with the risk's expected cost, probability times impact, then ask separately whether the project could survive the worst case.

Q. In Week 72, what is a politically exposed person, and why do banks care?

A. Someone who holds or held a prominent public role, or a close family member or associate of one. Banks apply enhanced checks because such positions carry a higher risk of corruption.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the contingency line is the most argued-over number in a development budget. Too low and the project looks attractive until the first bad month, when the overrun lands on your equity. Too high and the project looks too expensive to fund. A risk-based contingency replaces that argument with a stated level of confidence everyone can test. Figures today are hypothetical round numbers.

From a register to a range

In plain English: instead of one cost figure, think of the whole range of costs the project could end up with, and how likely each is.

The professional framing is a probability distribution of outturn cost. You take the base estimate, add each risk from the register with its probability and its range of impact, and combine them. Done by hand for a few risks it is simple counting, as Roman will show in two days. Done for many risks with ranges, it is a Monte Carlo simulation: a computer draws thousands of random combinations of the risks and records the total cost of each, producing a curve. From the curve you read percentiles. P50 is the cost the project has a 50 percent chance of coming in under. P80 is the cost it has an 80 percent chance of coming in under. P90, 90 percent.

The expected value, the average of all those outcomes, is usually above P50, because cost risks are lopsided: things rarely go much better than planned and occasionally go much worse.

What the choice does to the numbers

A worked example, hypothetical. Base cost of a project, excluding contingency, is 20,000,000 dollars. The risk analysis gives a P50 contingency of 400,000 dollars, an expected value of 590,000 dollars, a P80 of 1,200,000 dollars and a P90 of 1,200,000 dollars as well, because one large risk sits just above that level. Stabilised net operating income (NOI), rent less operating costs, is 1,500,000 dollars a year.

Contingency chosenTotal budgetYield on cost
P50, 400,000 dollars20,400,000 dollars7.35 percent
P80, 1,200,000 dollars21,200,000 dollars7.08 percent

Yield on cost is stabilised NOI divided by total cost, the measure from Week 10. Choosing P80 rather than P50 lowers the headline yield by about a quarter of a percentage point. That is the price of confidence, and it is visible.

Now the part the headline hides. Suppose the lender funds 65 percent of the budget, a commercial loan-to-cost limit, not a standard. At P50 the loan is 13,260,000 dollars and equity 7,140,000 dollars. At P80 the loan is 13,780,000 dollars and equity 7,420,000 dollars. The extra 800,000 dollars of contingency costs only 280,000 dollars of extra equity, because the lender funds most of it.

Then the bad case. Suppose risks worth 1,200,000 dollars actually happen. Under the P80 budget, the contingency covers them and the loan stays in balance. Under the P50 budget, the 400,000 dollar contingency is used up and 800,000 dollars of overrun remain. The loan was sized to the budget, so the lender will not fund the excess: the in-balance test from Week 40 requires you to deposit it. Equity rises from 7,140,000 to 7,940,000 dollars, an 11 percent increase, all at once, in the middle of construction, from you.

Say that out loud now.

Contingency inside the budget is shared with the lender. An overrun outside it is mine alone.

Returns and the timing of contingency

Contingency also has a timing. Risks are concentrated in certain phases, ground early, commissioning and lease-up late. A sensible model draws contingency down as risks are retired, and releases unused contingency only near completion. Unused contingency is not profit until the building is finished and the risks it covered have passed.

A second worked example, hypothetical, on equity returns. Suppose the project is sold on completion for 25,000,000 dollars. With a P80 budget that comes in exactly on budget, equity of 7,420,000 dollars earns a profit of 25,000,000 less 21,200,000, which is 3,800,000 dollars. With a P50 budget that suffers the 1,200,000 dollar bad case, total cost is also 21,200,000 dollars and profit is also 3,800,000 dollars, but it is earned on 7,940,000 dollars of equity, with 800,000 dollars injected late and unplanned. The profit is the same; the return on equity is lower, and the risk of not having the 800,000 dollars at all was yours throughout. These yields, loan ratios and returns are illustrations of method, not benchmarks.

The Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note. On your personal balance sheet, the gap between the contingency you budgeted and the contingency your risks really need is a contingent claim on your own liquidity. If you build at P50, you should hold personal liquidity, or committed equity from partners, at least equal to the gap between P50 and P80, or you have made a promise to the lender you may not be able to keep. Keep that number beside your guarantees in your personal review. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

Decision journals

This month's thread is the decision journal from Week 2. The contingency choice is one of the best decisions to record: write down the percentile you chose, the risks you believed drove it, and what you expected to happen. Date it.

At completion, open the entry and compare. Which risks happened, which did not, and which you never saw? Over three or four projects, that record tells you whether your estimates run optimistic, which no adviser can tell you as reliably as your own past self.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is budgeting contingency to make the yield look good, then funding the overrun from equity in the worst month of the project. The control is a risk-based contingency at a stated percentile, agreed with the lender, and personal or committed liquidity to cover the gap if you choose a lower one.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner applies a flat 5 or 10 percent to every project. Two projects of the same size can carry very different risks; the contingency should follow the register, not the habit.

Callback

In Week 51, Quincy and Nadia taught contingency structure, design contingency, construction contingency and owner's contingency, and cost-to-complete forecasting. The Monte Carlo view does not replace that structure. It tells you how big each bucket should be, and how confident you are that the buckets together will hold.

Recap

Contingency is a percentile: P50, P80 or P90 of a range of outturn costs drawn from the register. Higher confidence lowers the headline yield a little and costs equity only in proportion to the loan-to-cost. An overrun beyond contingency is funded by equity alone, at the worst time. Draw contingency down as risks retire, and journal the choice.

Next: LEX on The Rules: contractor default, termination, step-in and the cure notice.
checklist: I set contingency from the risk register, not from a flat percentage.
I can state the percentile my contingency represents.
I know my yield on cost at P50 and at P80.
I know how much equity an overrun beyond contingency would require, and when.
I hold liquidity or committed equity for the gap if I choose a low percentile.
I draw contingency down as risks retire and release it only near completion.
I record the contingency decision in my decision journal and review it at completion.
head: Field checklist
speak: A contingency is a confidence level I choose. From the risk register I build a range of outturn costs; a Monte Carlo simulation does it with thousands of random combinations. P50 is the cost I have an even chance of beating; P80, an 80 percent chance. On a 20,000,000 dollar base, P50 contingency of 400,000 dollars gives a yield on cost of 7.35 percent; P80 of 1,200,000 gives 7.08. That quarter point is the visible price of confidence. The hidden price runs the other way. Contingency inside the budget is mostly funded by the lender, so the extra 800,000 dollars costs only 280,000 of equity at 65 percent loan to cost. But if I budget at P50 and 1,200,000 dollars of risk happens, the 800,000 overrun is outside the loan, and I deposit it myself, mid-construction. So I choose a stated percentile, agree it with the lender, and record the choice in my decision journal.
terms: Monte Carlo simulation — a method that combines risks by drawing thousands of random outcomes, producing a range of possible results.
P80 — the value that a result has an 80 percent chance of not exceeding.
Yield on cost — stabilised net operating income divided by total development cost.

hostile.q: Your contingency is 1,200,000 dollars on a 20,000,000 dollar base, which is 6 percent. Your competitor shows 3 percent. Why is yours so high?
hostile.a: Because ours is the P80 of our own risk register, not a habit, and I can show you the register, the impacts and the distribution behind it. At 3 percent we would be near P50 on this project, which means an even chance of an overrun funded outside the loan. I would rather show you a slightly lower yield on cost and a budget that holds four times in five than a better headline that needs an equity call halfway through.

title: Contractor Default: Notice, Cure, Termination and Step-In
summary: Terminating a contractor is the most dangerous legal act an owner takes on a project, because a wrongful termination can make the owner the party in breach. The contract's default procedure, its cure periods, its insolvency provisions and its step-in and assignment rights decide whether you can replace a failing contractor cleanly.
body:
Removing a failing contractor is the most dangerous legal act an owner takes. Do it by the contract's procedure, step by step and in writing, or a wrongful termination can turn you into the party in breach.

Recall

Q. What is P80?

A. The value a result has an 80 percent chance of not exceeding. For contingency, it is the budget the project has an 80 percent chance of coming in under.

Q. In Week 78, what is the prevention principle?

A. A party cannot enforce a deadline it prevented the other from meeting. If the owner delayed the contractor and the contract cannot extend time, the date and the liquidated damages can fall away.

Q. In Week 72, what are sanctions, for a developer?

A. Legal restrictions imposed by governments on dealing with named persons, entities or countries. Dealing with a sanctioned party, even indirectly through a contractor or supplier, can carry severe penalties.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman's register tells you when a contractor is failing. This lesson is about what you are allowed to do about it. The instinct, when a contractor is late, unpaid subcontractors are calling and the site is half empty, is to throw it off the job. Courts in many common-law systems treat termination as a remedy of last resort. If you terminate without a right to do so, or without following the procedure, your termination can itself be treated as a repudiation, a refusal to perform the contract, which lets the contractor claim its lost profit on the whole remaining job. These are general concepts; the rules vary by jurisdiction and by contract form, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The default ladder in the contract

In plain English: the contract gives the contractor a warning and a chance to fix the problem before you can remove it.

The professional framing is the termination for default procedure. Standard forms, including those you met in Week 77, typically set out a ladder. First, a defined ground: persistent failure to proceed with due diligence, failure to remedy defective work, suspension without cause, failure to pay subcontractors, breach of a material obligation, or insolvency. Second, a notice to the contractor identifying the default, often with a copy to the surety. Third, a cure period, a stated number of days in which the contractor may remedy the default or start diligently to remedy it. Fourth, if the default is not cured, a second notice terminating the contractor's employment. The exact grounds, the number of days and whether a certifier or engineer must first confirm the default differ between forms and between editions; read your contract, not a summary of it.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A contractor on a 15,000,000 dollar job has had only a third of its planned labour on site for six weeks and has fallen 40 days behind the programme. The owner issues a default notice under the clause for failure to proceed with due diligence, citing the labour records and the programme. The contract gives 14 days to cure. On day 10 the contractor brings two more crews and presents a recovery programme. That may be a cure, or the beginning of one, and terminating on day 15 may be wrongful. The owner instead records the recovery commitments and monitors them weekly, with the right to issue a fresh notice if they slip.

Insolvency is its own ground, with its own limits

Most contracts make insolvency events, such as an administration, a receivership or a winding-up, a ground for termination, sometimes without a cure period. Be careful. In several jurisdictions insolvency law restricts or overrides clauses that allow a party to terminate merely because the other has entered an insolvency process, so that a business can be rescued [unverified — confirm independently]. Where that applies, you may need a different ground, such as an actual failure to perform, or the agreement of the insolvency officeholder. Ask counsel before relying on an insolvency clause.

Say that out loud now.

Ground, notice, cure, then termination. Skip a rung and I may be the one in breach.

Termination for convenience

Many owner-drafted contracts also allow termination for convenience: the owner may end the contract without any default, usually paying for work done, demobilisation and sometimes a stated fee for lost profit. It is a useful exit when the contractor's performance is poor but hard to prove as a default. It is not free, and courts in some places scrutinise its use in bad faith. A termination for convenience costs a known amount; a wrongful termination for default can cost an unknown one.

What you need after termination: step-in and assignment

Terminating is the easy part. Finishing is hard, and the right clauses make it possible.

  • Assignment of subcontracts: the right to take over the contractor's subcontracts and supply orders, so that the steel fabricator or the mechanical subcontractor keeps working for you.
  • Step-in rights: rights, usually in direct agreements or collateral warranties, for the owner or its lender to step into a contract with a subcontractor or consultant and continue it.
  • Delivery of documents and materials: an obligation to hand over drawings, calculations, records, warranties and materials on site or paid for off site, with licences to use the design.
  • Right to complete and recover: the right to engage others to complete and to recover the extra cost from the contractor or its surety, often with a final account after completion.

A second worked example, hypothetical. The owner terminates properly on a job with 5,000,000 dollars of unpaid balance. Without an assignment clause, the mechanical subcontractor, unpaid by the failed contractor, refuses to continue, its long-lead chillers sit in its yard, and re-ordering costs 22 weeks. With the clause, the owner pays the subcontractor directly for future work, the subcontractor continues, and the chillers arrive on schedule. The difference, at the 8,000 dollar daily cost of delay from Week 78, is about 1,200,000 dollars.

The surety and the lender must be inside the procedure

The surety's bond and the lender's loan both contain their own conditions. A termination that does not follow the bond's notice requirements may weaken the surety's obligation, as Week 79 showed. A termination that the lender did not approve may itself breach the loan agreement, because replacing the contractor is often a matter needing lender consent. Copy every notice to both, and agree the completion route before anything is final.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, as construction counsel, before any default or termination notice is sent.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is wrongful termination: acting on frustration, skipping a notice, cutting a cure period short or relying on an insolvency clause the law will not enforce, and so handing the contractor a claim for its lost profit. The control is counsel's review of every notice, a dated evidence file for each ground, and strict adherence to the contract's days and forms.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner tells the contractor to leave site in an angry meeting. Words spoken in a meeting can be treated as a termination. Say nothing about termination aloud; put the procedure in writing, through counsel.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught how to instruct professionals and keep records. A default file is the test of those habits: dated labour returns, programme updates, correspondence and photographs, assembled as events happen, are what make a termination stand. Records built afterwards look like what they are.

Recap

Terminate only on a defined ground, by written notice, after the cure period, through counsel. Treat insolvency clauses with care, because insolvency law may limit them. Keep termination for convenience as a known-cost exit. Make sure the contract gives you assignment, step-in, documents and the right to complete. Keep the surety and the lender inside every step.

Next: Roman on The Numbers: reverse engineering a contingency figure to find the confidence it really buys.
checklist: I know the grounds, notices and cure periods in my contract's default clause.
I keep a dated evidence file for every potential ground of default.
No default or termination notice leaves without counsel's review.
I copy every default notice to the surety and the lender.
I know whether insolvency law in my jurisdiction limits insolvency termination clauses.
My contract gives me assignment of subcontracts, step-in rights, documents and the right to complete.
I never speak of termination aloud in a meeting.
head: Field checklist
speak: Removing a failing contractor is the most dangerous legal act an owner takes, because a wrongful termination can be treated as my own repudiation and give the contractor a claim for its lost profit on the whole job. So I climb the contract's ladder: a defined ground, such as failure to proceed diligently, a written default notice copied to the surety, the full cure period, and only then a termination notice, all reviewed by counsel. If the contractor starts a genuine recovery inside the cure period, I may have to monitor rather than terminate. Insolvency clauses need care, because insolvency law in some places limits them. Termination for convenience is a known-cost exit. And termination is useless without the clauses to finish: assignment of subcontracts, step-in rights, handover of drawings and materials, and the right to complete and recover. I never speak of termination aloud in a meeting.
terms: Termination for default — ending a contractor's employment for a defined breach, after notice and any cure period required by the contract.
Cure period — the time a defaulting party is given after notice to remedy the default before termination is allowed.
Step-in rights — rights, usually in direct agreements, for the owner or lender to take over a subcontract or appointment and continue it.

hostile.q: You terminated us on day 15 of a 14-day cure period while we were bringing crews back. That is repudiation. Why should we not claim our lost profit?
hostile.a: I will not argue it with you here; it will be answered in writing through counsel. What I can say is that the notice set out the default with dated labour records, the cure period ran in full, and on day 14 the labour on site was still below the recovery programme you yourself presented. If the facts are as you say, the contract's dispute procedure is where that is tested. Meanwhile I am asking you to hand over the documents and materials the contract requires.

title: Reverse Engineering the Confidence a Contingency Buys
summary: Start from a contingency figure already in a budget and work backward to the probability that it will be enough. Three risks from a register are combined by hand into every possible outcome, the outcomes are ranked, and the contingency is read as a percentile. Then the same table shows what a bond does to the answer.
body:
A contingency figure in a budget is a silent claim about confidence. Work backward from it, through the risks it is meant to cover, and you can say exactly how likely it is to be enough.

Recall

Q. What must happen before an owner may terminate a contractor for default under most standard forms?

A. A defined ground, a written default notice, and the expiry of the cure period without a cure, followed by a termination notice, all in the contract's required form.

Q. In Week 78, how did Priya work backward from a liquidated damages rate?

A. She divided the cap by the rate to find the day delay becomes free to the contractor, then compared the rate with the owner's true daily cost of delay to see the risk the owner kept.

Q. In Week 72, why does a developer check the beneficial ownership of its contractors and suppliers?

A. To know who it is really dealing with, to avoid sanctioned or corrupt parties, and to meet the banking and anti-money-laundering expectations of lenders.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most budgets carry a contingency figure nobody can explain. A lender's monitor will ask what it covers. You will be able to answer with a number: this contingency has a stated chance of covering our identified risks. Today we start from a finished outcome, a contingency already written into a budget, and work backward. A computer does this with thousands of draws in a Monte Carlo simulation; by hand, with three risks, you can see every step. All figures are hypothetical round numbers.

Step 1: the finished outcome and the risks behind it

The budget for a 20,000,000 dollar project carries a contingency of 1,500,000 dollars, 7.5 percent. The risk register's top three priced risks, assumed independent of each other, are these.

RiskProbabilityImpact if it happensExpected cost
A. Poor ground needing extra foundations30 percent800,000 dollars240,000 dollars
B. Contractor default, owner's net cost10 percent1,500,000 dollars150,000 dollars
C. Weather delay50 percent400,000 dollars200,000 dollars
Total590,000 dollars

The expected cost, 590,000 dollars, is the long-run average. It tells you the contingency is well above average, but not how confident you are.

Step 2: list every combination

Each risk either happens or does not, so three risks give eight combinations. Multiply the probabilities for each. For the combination where none happens: 0.7 times 0.9 times 0.5, which is 0.315.

CombinationProbabilityTotal cost
None0.3150
C only0.7 times 0.9 times 0.5 = 0.315400,000
A only0.3 times 0.9 times 0.5 = 0.135800,000
A and C0.1351,200,000
B only0.7 times 0.1 times 0.5 = 0.0351,500,000
B and C0.0351,900,000
A and B0.3 times 0.1 times 0.5 = 0.0152,300,000
A, B and C0.0152,700,000

Check that the probabilities add to 1: 0.315 plus 0.315 plus 0.135 plus 0.135 plus 0.035 plus 0.035 plus 0.015 plus 0.015 is 1.000. If they do not, a step is wrong.

Step 3: rank and accumulate

Sort by total cost and add the probabilities as you go. That running total is the chance the cost will not exceed each level.

  1. 0 dollars: 31.5 percent.
  2. Up to 400,000 dollars: 63.0 percent.
  3. Up to 800,000 dollars: 76.5 percent.
  4. Up to 1,200,000 dollars: 90.0 percent.
  5. Up to 1,500,000 dollars: 93.5 percent.
  6. Up to 1,900,000 dollars: 97.0 percent.
  7. Up to 2,300,000 dollars: 98.5 percent.
  8. Up to 2,700,000 dollars: 100 percent.

Now read the finished outcome. A contingency of 1,500,000 dollars covers the identified risks with a probability of 93.5 percent. That is the claim the budget was silently making.

Say that out loud now.

Sort the outcomes, add the probabilities, and read the contingency as a percentile.

Step 4: work back to the percentile you want

Reverse the question. What is the smallest contingency giving at least 80 percent? From the list, 800,000 dollars gives 76.5 percent, not enough; 1,200,000 dollars gives 90 percent. So P80, and here P90 as well, is 1,200,000 dollars. The P50 is 400,000 dollars. Notice the jumps. With few risks, the curve moves in steps, and one large, unlikely risk, the contractor default, sits in the tail above 1,200,000 dollars. The extra 300,000 dollars that takes the budget from 1,200,000 to 1,500,000 dollars buys only 3.5 percentage points of confidence. It is covering one specific tail: default without ground trouble.

Step 5: what a bond does to the table

A second worked example, hypothetical. Suppose the contractor provides a performance and payment bond that, from Week 79's calculation, reduces the owner's net cost of a default from 1,500,000 to 300,000 dollars, the delay and items the bond would not cover. Re-run risk B at 300,000 dollars.

  1. New totals: none 0; C 400,000; B 300,000; B and C 700,000; A 800,000; A and C 1,200,000; A and B 1,100,000; A, B and C 1,500,000.
  2. Sorted with running totals: 0 at 31.5 percent; 300,000 at 35.0; 400,000 at 66.5; 700,000 at 70.0; 800,000 at 83.5; 1,100,000 at 85.0; 1,200,000 at 98.5; 1,500,000 at 100.
  3. P80 is now 800,000 dollars, and 1,200,000 dollars gives 98.5 percent.

The bond removed most of the tail. The same 1,500,000 dollar contingency now covers every identified combination, or the budget could carry about 1,200,000 dollars and still be near 98 percent. Set that saving beside the bond premium from Week 79, roughly 1 percent of the contract, and you can see, in one table, what the bond buys.

One more way to read the same table. The chance of an overrun at all, with no contingency, is 68.5 percent, because only the no-risk combination costs nothing. The chance of needing more than the expected cost of 590,000 dollars is 37 percent. Those two figures are worth saying aloud to anyone who suggests that a contingency equal to the expected cost is prudent. It leaves better than one chance in three of reaching into equity.

Step 6: the limits of the method

Three warnings. First, the risks were assumed independent. In reality they often move together: bad ground causes delay, and delay strains a weak contractor. Correlated risks fatten the tail, so an independent model understates the high percentiles. Second, only identified risks are counted; the risks nobody listed are not in the table, which is why many owners hold a separate allowance for the unknown. Third, the inputs are judgements. Ask your engineer and quantity surveyor for them, and record who gave each one.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor, on impacts; risk analyst or cost consultant, for a full Monte Carlo model on any project of real size.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating an independent-risk model as exact: a 93.5 percent figure from three uncorrelated risks can be badly optimistic once delay, ground and contractor failure are linked. The control is to test a correlated case, where one risk raises the probability of another, and to hold an allowance for risks not yet identified.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner adds all the impacts together, 2,700,000 dollars, and calls that the contingency, or adds the expected values, 590,000 dollars, and calls that enough. The first buys certainty at a price nobody will fund; the second leaves a better-than-one-in-three chance of an overrun. The percentile lies between them, and you choose it.

Callback

In Week 44, I taught tornado charts: which single input moves the result most. Step 5 is the same question asked of the contingency. The contractor default was the risk that dominated the tail, and changing its impact moved the percentiles more than anything else. Find the risk that owns the tail and treat it first.

Recap

Start from the contingency in the budget. List the risks, list every combination with its probability, sort by cost and accumulate. Read the contingency as a percentile, here 93.5 percent, and find P50 and P80 by reading back. Re-run with a mitigation, such as a bond, to see what it buys. Remember correlation and the unknown.

Next: Roman in The Room: the monthly risk review the week a contractor starts to show signs of distress.
checklist: I can say what percentile the contingency in my budget represents.
I list the top risks with probability and impact from named professionals.
I check that combination probabilities add to 1.
I find P50 and P80 by sorting outcomes and accumulating probabilities.
I re-run the table with each major mitigation to see what it buys.
I test a correlated case where one risk raises the chance of another.
I hold a separate allowance for risks not yet identified.
head: Field checklist
speak: A contingency in a budget is a silent claim about confidence, so I work backward from it. Take a 1,500,000 dollar contingency on a 20,000,000 dollar project, and three risks: ground at 30 percent and 800,000 dollars, contractor default at 10 percent and 1,500,000, weather at 50 percent and 400,000. The expected cost is 590,000. Three risks give eight combinations; I multiply the probabilities, check they add to one, sort by cost and add up as I go. The running total reaches 93.5 percent at 1,500,000 dollars, so that is what the budget buys. P50 is 400,000 and P80 is 1,200,000. Then I re-run with a bond that cuts the default cost to 300,000: P80 falls to 800,000 and the same budget covers every identified case. Two warnings: real risks are correlated, which fattens the tail, and the risks nobody listed are not in the table.
terms: Percentile — the value below which a stated share of outcomes falls; P80 is the 80th percentile.
Cumulative probability — the running total of probabilities, read as the chance a result will not exceed a given level.
Correlation — the tendency of two risks to happen together, which makes bad outcomes more likely than an independent model shows.

hostile.q: You say your contingency covers 93.5 percent of outcomes. Isn't that a precise-looking number built on guesses?
hostile.a: Yes, and I would rather show you the guesses than hide them. Each probability and impact came from our engineer or quantity surveyor, and their names are on the register. The model assumes the risks are independent, which flatters the tail, so I have also run a correlated case, where poor ground raises the chance of contractor default; there the same contingency gives about 85 percent. We hold a separate allowance for risks nobody has identified. The number is a structured judgement, not a guarantee.

title: The Risk Review the Week the Contractor Wobbles
summary: A scene: two subcontractors report late payment, the contractor's site manager has resigned and the contractor asks for an early release of retainage. Your amber trigger has fired. You meet the contractor's managing director with the lender's monitor present. The lines to say, the lines never to say, and how to hold your state.
body:
When an amber trigger fires, the meeting you hold next is not a negotiation and not an accusation. It is a fact-finding session with a contractor you still need, run so that you learn the truth and keep every option open.

Recall

Q. In Roman's reverse engineering, what did the performance bond do to the contingency table?

A. It cut the owner's net cost of a contractor default, removing most of the tail, so the same contingency covered every identified combination and P80 fell from 1,200,000 to 800,000 dollars.

Q. In Week 78, what is the question behind a consultant's request for a low cap?

A. Will you protect our insurance? Answering it turns a fight about liability into a practical discussion about policy limits.

Q. In Week 72, what is the right response to an offer of an improper payment to speed an approval?

A. Decline it plainly, record it, report it under your policy and to counsel, and never let a third party pay it on your behalf. Anti-bribery laws can reach payments made through agents.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the Carillion case showed that the months between the first warning and the failure are the only months in which an owner can act. This is the first meeting in those months. Handle it badly and you either miss the warning or accelerate the failure you fear. The numbers are hypothetical.

The scene

Month 9 of an 18-month, 18,000,000 dollar contract. In one fortnight: two subcontractors have told your project manager that payments are 45 days late; the contractor's experienced site manager has resigned; and the contractor has written asking for half of the 900,000 dollars of retainage to be released early, citing cash flow. Your register sets two subcontractor complaints, or an early retainage request, as amber. Both have fired. You have invited the contractor's managing director to a meeting. The lender's monitor attends at your invitation, as the loan agreement allows.

The question behind the question

The managing director's request for retainage is a question: will you lend us money? Retainage is your security for completion; releasing it early is an unsecured loan to a contractor with a cash problem. Behind that sits a bigger question: is this a timing problem on one job, or a company in trouble across many?

Your own question behind the question is the one to keep in front of you: if this contractor failed in the next three months, how ready am I?

The lines to say

Open with the purpose. "Thank you for coming. I want to understand your position fully, because our projects depend on each other. Nothing in this meeting is a notice under the contract."

Ask for facts, not reassurance. "Can you walk us through your payment position with subcontractors on this job, and when the two late payments will clear?" "Who replaces the site manager, and when do they start?" "Is the cash pressure specific to this project, or wider?"

On retainage. "Retainage is our protection for completion, and I can't release it early. What I can do is look at anything that helps cash flow without reducing that protection: paying a verified stored-materials claim promptly, or paying certain subcontractors directly with your agreement, against a clear accounting." Direct payment and joint cheques must be permitted by the contract and checked by counsel, and they change who carries risk; use them only on advice.

On next steps. "We'll verify subcontractor payment before each draw from now on, and we'd like weekly labour returns for the next month. Let's meet again in two weeks."

Say that out loud now.

I want the facts, I cannot lend you my security, and here is what I can do.

The lines never to say

Never say: "If you can't pay your subs, we'll find someone who can." It is a threat you are not ready to carry out, it may be read as an intention to terminate, and it can trigger the very panic among subcontractors and lenders that sinks a contractor.

Never say: "Don't worry, we'll release the retainage if it helps." Once released, it is gone, and a surety may argue that the early release reduced the security it relied on.

Never say anything about the contractor's position to its subcontractors that you cannot prove. Rumour from the owner can move a contractor's suppliers onto cash-only terms overnight.

If the answers are good

Amber is not a verdict. If the managing director produces a payment schedule that clears both subcontractors within a week, names an experienced replacement site manager starting on a fixed date, and shows that the cash pressure came from one late-paying client elsewhere with a settlement agreed, then say so plainly: "Thank you; that answers my questions. We'll keep the extra checks for a month and then review." Move the register back toward green on evidence, not on relief, and record what changed. An owner who escalates on criteria must also de-escalate on criteria, or the contractor learns that the triggers mean nothing.

When to stay silent

After you ask whether the pressure is wider than this job, wait. Do not offer the managing director an easy answer such as "I assume it is just this project?" The length and content of the answer, or the absence of one, is the most important information in the room.

Stay silent, too, when the monitor asks technical questions about billing against work in place. Let the monitor's independence do its work.

Holding your state

Your operations background is the asset here. You have run calm control rooms while a system was under stress: acknowledge the alarm, gather data, follow the procedure written in advance, escalate on criteria, not on mood. Do the same. Keep your voice even and your questions short. A visibly anxious owner tells the contractor, the monitor and later the lender that the project is out of control.

After the meeting: the money

A worked example, hypothetical. The contractor's answers are partial: the site manager's replacement is unnamed and the cash pressure is described as across several jobs. You update the register. Probability of contractor default moves from 10 percent to 25 percent. Using Week 79's numbers, the owner's net cost of a default, with bonds, is about 300,000 dollars plus delay. A second worked example: suppose readiness work, a second contractor briefed to price at short notice, an inventory of drawings and materials, and a call with the surety, costs 40,000 dollars and cuts the restart time after a default from 20 weeks to 10. At 8,000 dollars a day, ten weeks saved is 560,000 dollars. At a 25 percent probability, that is 140,000 dollars of expected saving for 40,000 dollars spent. You spend it.

Then you write a short note to the lender: what fired, what you learned, what you are doing, and the next review date. The lender should hear it from you before it hears it from the monitor.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, before any change to payment arrangements or any notice; surety's representative, informed in writing.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is acting on emotion at amber: either lending the contractor your security to make the problem go away, or threatening termination you are not ready for. Both make failure more likely and recovery harder. The control is the procedure you wrote when you set the trigger: verify, monitor, prepare, escalate on criteria.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner hears "temporary cash-flow issue" and relaxes. Temporary is a claim, not a fact. Verify it with payment records and labour returns over the next weeks.

Callback

In Week 40, Ford and Roman's composite case showed a contractor's request to reduce retainage early as a classic sign of cash stress, one that the developer ignored. This scene is the same signal, met the right way: the request is declined, and the warning is acted on while there is still time.

Recap

Amber fired: late subcontractor payments, a lost site manager and an early retainage request. Meet to find facts, with the monitor present. Decline to release your security, offer help that keeps it intact, verify payment and labour, and prepare for default while hoping not to need it. Hold your state, stay silent after the hard question, update the register and tell the lender first.

Next: Kema on the Week 80 review: six questions, Cole's Auditor's Chair on a risk register, and the boardroom drill.
checklist: I hold a fact-finding meeting as soon as an amber trigger fires.
I say at the start that the meeting is not a notice under the contract.
I decline early release of retainage and offer help that keeps my security intact.
I verify subcontractor payment directly before each draw at amber.
I ask whether the contractor's pressure is wider than my project, then wait.
I spend on readiness when its expected saving exceeds its cost.
I tell the lender in writing what fired and what I am doing, before the monitor does.
head: Field checklist
speak: When an amber trigger fires, two subcontractors paid late, a site manager gone and a request to release retainage early, I hold a fact-finding meeting, with the lender's monitor present, and I say at the start that it is not a notice under the contract. I ask for facts: the payment position, the replacement site manager, and whether the cash pressure is wider than my job. Then I wait for the answer. I do not release retainage, because it is my security and releasing it is an unsecured loan, but I offer help that keeps it intact, such as prompt payment of verified claims. I never threaten termination I am not ready for. Afterwards I update the register. If default probability rises to 25 percent, spending 40,000 dollars on readiness to save ten weeks of delay worth 560,000 dollars is an easy decision. And I tell the lender what fired before the monitor does.
terms: Retainage — a share of each payment held back by the owner until completion, as security for the contractor's performance.
Joint cheque — a payment made out to both the contractor and a subcontractor, so the subcontractor is paid from it directly.
Readiness work — preparation for a possible contractor default, such as a briefed replacement and an inventory of documents and materials.

hostile.q: Two of your contractor's subs are unpaid and you have not told me. Why am I hearing it from my monitor?
hostile.a: You should have heard it from me first, and from now on you will. The trigger fired this week. I met the contractor's managing director on Tuesday with your monitor present. We now verify subcontractor payment before each draw, the retainage stays where it is, and I have briefed a second contractor and spoken to the surety. My written note to you is going today, with the next review date.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 80 Review: A Project That Survives Its Worst Single Failure
summary: Six questions test the week: the N-1 test, the risk register and triggers, Rule 80, contingency as a percentile, termination for default and the amber-trigger meeting. Cole takes the Auditor's Chair to read a hypothetical risk register as a hostile auditor would, then a two-minute boardroom drill.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: run the project so it survives the loss of any single element, with every significant risk named, owned, watched for a trigger and funded at a confidence level you chose.

Recall

Q. What is the question behind a contractor's request to release retainage early?

A. Will you lend us money? Retainage is your security for completion, so releasing it early is an unsecured loan to a contractor under cash pressure.

Q. In Week 78, why should a consequential loss exclusion be a list?

A. Because the phrase has often been read narrowly, so a bare exclusion may not exclude lost rent or profit. A list removes the argument.

Q. In Week 72, why is reputation treated as an integrity risk for a developer?

A. Because lenders, partners and authorities decide whether to deal with you partly on trust, and one association with corruption, sanctions or dirty money can close doors that no contract can reopen.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you can answer these six questions aloud without notes, you can sit with a lender's monitor and an investment committee and show that your project is managed as a system, not hoped through. Answer each before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. State the N-1 test for a project.

Answer: The project must survive the loss of any single element, contractor, lender, critical supplier, key consultant, pending approval or you, with a written plan to continue without it.

Question 2. What columns make a risk register work?

Answer: Cause and effect, probability and impact in dollars and days before and after the response, one named owner, the response, a trigger with a threshold, and the date last reviewed.

Question 3. State Rule 80.

Answer: Treat the failure of your most important counterparty as a planned event: name it in the register, give it an owner, watch its leading indicators against written triggers, and keep a tested plan to continue without it.

Question 4. Why does a contingency set at P50 cost you more in a bad case than one set at P80?

Answer: Contingency inside the budget is largely funded by the loan. An overrun beyond it is outside the loan, so you deposit it from equity, all at once, in the middle of construction.

Question 5. With three independent risks, how do you find the confidence a contingency buys?

Answer: List all eight combinations, multiply the probabilities, check they total 1, sort by cost and accumulate. The running total at the contingency figure is its percentile.

Question 6. What can make a termination for default wrongful?

Answer: No valid ground, a defective or missing notice, cutting the cure period short, relying on an insolvency clause the law restricts, or terminating aloud in a meeting. A wrongful termination can be treated as the owner's own repudiation.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Roman brought the grid operator's N-1 rule to the project and built the register around owners and triggers. Ford and Roman took Carillion, 2018, and gave Rule 80. Sage showed contingency as a percentile and what it does to equity and yield. LEX set out the default ladder, step-in and assignment. Roman reverse engineered the confidence a contingency buys. Roman ran the amber-trigger meeting.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 80 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair: read this hypothetical extract from a risk register as a hostile auditor would. Find the defects before reading on.

Project Risk Register, version 1, issued at financial close. Risk 1: Ground conditions. Likelihood medium, impact medium. Owner: Contractor. Response: contractor bears risk under the contract. Risk 2: Contractor insolvency. Likelihood low. Owner: Project team. Response: monitor. Risk 3: Cost overrun. Likelihood medium, impact high. Owner: Developer. Response: contingency of 5 percent. Risk 4: Delay. Owner: Project manager. Response: liquidated damages. Total risks identified: 4. Next review: as required.

The defects. First, it is version 1, issued at financial close, with a next review of as required: a document written for the lender, not a tool in use. Second, risks are scored medium and low with no probability or impact in dollars and days, so nothing in it can size a contingency. Third, risk 1 is owned by the contractor and answered by the contract, which is Rule 78's illusion of transfer: it says nothing about whether the contractor could carry the cost, or about the owner's exposure if it cannot. Fourth, risk 2 is owned by the project team, which is nobody, and answered by monitor, with no indicator, no threshold and no plan, the exact failure Rule 80 exists to prevent. Fifth, risk 3 is a symptom, not a cause; cost overrun is what happens when other risks occur, and a flat 5 percent contingency is not linked to any distribution, so its confidence level is unknown. Sixth, risk 4 relies on liquidated damages, with no mention of the cap, the gap between the rate and the true daily cost of delay, or the prevention principle. Seventh, four risks on a construction project is not credible; the register omits approvals, supply chain, key people, weather, interest rate and the developer itself. And there is no N-1 analysis of single points of failure at all.

Then the auditor asks for evidence. For each risk: who assessed it, from what data, and when it was last reviewed. For the contingency: the calculation and the percentile. For the contractor: the financial review at award, the bond and the replacement plan. For the delay: the liquidated damages working. If any of these does not exist, the register describes intentions, not controls.

The boardroom drill

Stand up and explain this week to an investment committee in two minutes. Start a timer.

Model answer: "We run this project the way a grid operator runs a power system: it must survive the loss of any single element. We have tested that against the contractor, the lender, our critical suppliers, our consultants and our own key people, and each has a written continuation plan. Our register has one named owner per risk, impacts in dollars and days, and a trigger for each of the top ten, reviewed monthly in its own meeting. Contractor failure is a planned event: a financial review at award, performance and payment bonds, assignment and step-in rights, and amber and red triggers on subcontractor payment and billing. Our contingency is the P80 of the register, agreed with the lender, so a bad case is funded inside the loan rather than by a surprise equity call. When a trigger fires, the response is already written, and the lender hears it from us first."

Score your answer. Did you name the N-1 test? Did you give contingency as a percentile? Did you describe at least one trigger and its response? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a risk system that exists for the lender's file rather than for decisions. The control is the monthly review, one owner per risk, triggers with written responses and a contingency tied to a stated confidence level.

The beginner's mistake

Writing down risks and believing that is managing them. A risk is managed only when someone owns it, watches a trigger and has a decision already made for when it fires.

Callback

In Week 4, Kema taught the physiology of stress on shift work: name the alarm, slow the breathing when parked, act on procedure. The risk system is the same idea for a project. You write the procedure in a calm month so that, in the worst week, you are executing a plan rather than inventing one.

Recap

Survive any single failure. Register every significant risk with owner, impact, response and trigger, and review it monthly. Treat counterparty failure as a planned event under Rule 80. Choose contingency as a percentile and fund the gap if you choose low. Terminate only by the contract's ladder. Meet amber triggers with facts, not threats.

terms: Single point of failure — an element whose loss alone would stop the project.
Inherent and residual risk — a risk's size before and after the planned response is applied.
Unknown-risk allowance — a reserve held for risks not yet identified, separate from contingency for listed risks.

hostile.q: Your register was updated last month. How do I know it is not just a document for us?
hostile.a: Ask any risk owner on it what their trigger is and what they do when it fires; each can tell you without notes. Then look at the change log: in the last three months two risks closed, three were added and the contractor risk moved to amber, with the meeting notes and the actions taken. The contingency forecast is re-run from the register every month. If you find a risk with no owner or no trigger, I want to know.
